chief_complaint: proteinuria, hematuria, and facial rash in young female
hpi_details: A 22-year-old female presents to the clinic with proteinuria, hematuria, and a facial rash. The symptoms started recently and have gradually worsened.
ideas: thinks it might be lupus, since her aunt has the same condition
concerns: She is worried the rash will permanently scar her face right before her college graduation.
expectations: She hopes to leave with a soothing topical cream for her cheeks and a prescription for antibiotics.

available_results.value: 3+ protein with dysmorphic RBCs and red blood cell casts

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Lupus Nephritis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes prompt renal biopsy to classify disease severity, followed by induction immunosuppression (systemic corticosteroids plus mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide) tailored to the biopsy class, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: proteinuria, hematuria, and facial rash in young female
Key HPI features: A 22-year-old female presents to the clinic with proteinuria, hematuria, and a facial rash. The symptoms started recently and have gradually worsened.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 142/90, HR 88, low-grade fever 37.8C. Malar (butterfly) rash across the cheeks and nasal bridge, sparing the nasolabial folds; mild bilateral ankle edema; no active synovitis. Labs: Urinalysis with 3+ protein, dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts; 24-hour urine protein 3.5 g; serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL; low C3/C4 complement; positive ANA (high titer) and anti-dsDNA antibodies.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Lupus Nephritis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Other primary glomerulonephritis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rapidly rising creatinine — suggests aggressive (proliferative) lupus nephritis needing urgent biopsy.
management_principles: Obtain a renal biopsy promptly to classify lupus nephritis (ISN/RPS class) and guide immunosuppression
Start induction immunosuppression per biopsy class -- typically high-dose corticosteroids plus mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide for proliferative (Class III/IV) disease
Add hydroxychloroquine (renal-protective in all SLE patients) and an ACE inhibitor/ARB for proteinuria; refer to rheumatology and nephrology for combined management
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for Kidney Disease

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: proteinuria, hematuria, and facial rash in young female

A 22-year-old female presents with several weeks of foamy, dark urine and a facial rash across her cheeks that worsens with sun exposure. Also reports mild joint aches and fatigue. Denies fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 142/90, HR 88, low-grade fever 37.8C. Malar (butterfly) rash across the cheeks and nasal bridge, sparing the nasolabial folds; mild bilateral ankle edema; no active synovitis. Labs: Urinalysis with 3+ protein, dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts; 24-hour urine protein 3.5 g; serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL; low C3/C4 complement; positive ANA (high titer) and anti-dsDNA antibodies.
reference_soap.assessment: Lupus nephritis (likely proliferative, ISN/RPS Class III/IV) in a patient with new systemic lupus erythematosus, based on the malar rash, active urine sediment, heavy proteinuria, low complement, and positive ANA/anti-dsDNA.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Obtain a renal biopsy promptly to classify lupus nephritis and guide immunosuppression. 2. Start induction therapy with high-dose corticosteroids plus mycophenolate mofetil (or cyclophosphamide) based on the biopsy class. 3. Add hydroxychloroquine and an ACE inhibitor/ARB for proteinuria. 4. Refer to rheumatology and nephrology for combined management and monitor renal function, complement, and anti-dsDNA titers.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Lupus Nephritis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Lupus Nephritis
Implement evidence-based management plan: Renal biopsy, systemic corticosteroids, Mycophenolate Mofetil

teaching.one_liner: Kidney involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus, where immune complexes deposit in the glomeruli, causing proteinuria and hematuria, often alongside the classic facial rash.
red_flags: Rapidly rising creatinine — suggests aggressive (proliferative) lupus nephritis needing urgent biopsy

must_ask.say: Have you had a rash across your cheeks and nose?
Have you noticed blood or foam in your urine?
Does sunlight make your rash worse?

exam.finding: Blood pressure 142/90 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Well-demarcated erythematous maculopapular rash across bilateral cheeks and nasal bridge sparing the nasolabial folds; no petechiae, ecchymoses, or ulcerations.
No conjunctival pallor, scleral icterus, or periorbital edema noted.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation without crackles, wheezes, or pleural friction rubs.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or pericardial friction rubs.
Abdomen is soft, flat, and non-tender throughout with no palpable masses, organomegaly, or suprapubic distension.
No tenderness elicited upon gentle percussion over bilateral costovertebral angles.
Mild 1+ pitting edema noted over bilateral ankles and dorsum of feet; no pretibial erythema.
Bilateral proximal interphalangeal joints, wrists, and knees are without warmth, erythema, swelling, or active synovitis, with full passive and active range of motion.
